newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Hundreds of Zaire troops hand over arms to rebels.
newsitem.headline: Hundreds of Zaire troops hand over arms to rebels.

text.p: Hundreds of Zairean government troops handed their weapons over to victorious rebels on Monday in the city of Kisangani as the central government told its citizens not to panic over the military defeat.

Around 300 soldiers, some in tattered green uniform but others in civilian clothes, handed over their arms at a military camp 10 km (six miles) outside Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city and a major diamond and gold centre.

In the government-held capital of Kinshasa, the embattled government appealed to residents not to panic in the face of relentless rebel advances but travel agents reported a rush of flight bookings by Zaireans trying to flee the spreading war.

A statement, issued after an emergency cabinet meeting, said that the battle for Zaire's strategic third city of Kisangani had sparked the rumours, adding that the city had fallen on Saturday to well-armed Ugandan troops.
Zaire accuses Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi of backing the rebels. All three deny the charge.
Kisangani, the biggest prize in this civil war, was captured on Saturday with little resistance from Zaire's ragged army backed by Serb mercenaries and Rwandan Hutu allies.

One minister told Reuters that President Mobutu Sese Seko had telephoned twice during the cabinet meeting from his hospital bed in Europe, where he has spent most of his time since prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland in August.

"The situation created following the battle for Kisangani has given rise over the past 48 hours to all sorts of speculation, particularly in Kinshasa where fanciful rumours have circulated both about the president's state of health and the security of people and property in the capital," it said.
"The government invites the people not to panic as this is both unjustified and fed by pure rumour."
Residents in Kisangani say that the city, headquarters for army operations in the war zone, fell to rebels after Zairean soldiers looted what they could and fled.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has called for face-to-face talks with Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 and has dominated the sprawling and chaotic nation since then. Opponents accuse him of ruining one of Africa's potentially richest countries.
Rumours on Saturday -- in government circles and more widely in the capital -- suggested Mobutu had died.
France said on Monday that Mobutu's health was "a source of concern" in the clearest indication so far that the cancer-stricken ruler's physical condition is declining as fast as his grip on power.
As Tutsi-led rebels advance relentlessly through eastern Zaire, Mobutu has been convalescing from prostate cancer at his luxury French Riviera villa.

A spokesman there said the 66-year-old president was taken to Princess Grace hospital in Monte Carlo on Sunday afternoon for "additional treatment" but suggested he might be released as early as Tuesday morning.

Kinshasa residents reported sporadic gunshots overnight on Sunday around the teeming capital, where rumours of an imminent coup attempt are rife. In one incident, armed men opened fire from a car in the opposition stronghold of Limete.
In Kisangani, surrendering soldiers showed no signs of ill-treatment, lounging at the camp where some were based prior to the retreat at the weekend.

"We have put them (the soldiers) in these camps to teach them what our struggle is about. We will educate them and retrain them to decide which are fit to be part of the Alliance," said rebel commander Joseph Kabila.
There were no weapons to be seen at the base.
One Zairean soldier Jean-Philippe Mgunga said he decided to stay at the camp when other soldiers fled last weekend.
"We want change. Why flee?," Mgunga said.
Kisangani residents, in festivity mood, wore white bandanas or stuck tiny white flags in their bicycles on Monday in a show of solidarity with the rebels.
